item.title: Meteoectasis: A Word for the Impact That Leaves No Trace of the Impact
item.description:
Author & Lead Researcher:
Francisco Javier Jiménez Gómez
Independent Intellectual Property Owner


Presented under the institutional umbrella of:
BRISECOM S.L.
A specialized research and thinking laboratory dedicated to algorithmic ethics, AI governance, and human-centric technology intelligence.


30 October 2026



The word I am proposing in this article is meteoectasis, and I want to be clear from the first line about what it is and what it is not.

It is not a new physical mechanism. The physics it describes is in the literature, simulated in hydrocodes, and measured in isotopic ratios. It is a name for a state — the state a body reaches when it has been hit so hard that it stops being itself, and simultaneously not hard enough for anything to be destroyed. The full paper is in the LAIA repository and on laia.brisecom.org.

Why bother naming something that already has a description? Because the description is a periphrasis, and a periphrasis is where modelling errors hide.

The gap between two words

Planetary science has good words for the extremes.

Hit-and-run is precise: the impactor hits, survives, and leaves. The target takes a glancing blow and the projectile is still a projectile afterwards. Catastrophic disruption is equally precise: the target is torn apart and what remains is a family of fragments.

In between, everything is accretion. And accretion is a quantity word. It says that mass moved from one body to another. It says nothing whatsoever about the state of the material afterwards.

Consider two events that both count as accretion:

  • A planetesimal hits a protoplanet, sticks, and remains a chemically distinct body embedded in the target’s mantle.
  • A planetesimal hits a protoplanet, is entirely melted, expands thermally, and flows into the target’s magma ocean until nothing distinguishes its atoms from the target’s.

In the first case the target’s composition is a sum of inherited parts. In the second it is a mixture. Both are called “accreted”. For a modeller, the difference is enormous: the first produces a body with isotopic anomalies, the second does not.

What the word means

Meteoectasis — from Greek metéōron, “celestial body”, and éktasis, “expansion, dilatation” — is the process in which an impactor is integrated into a larger target at intermediate energy, with three conditions all met:

  1. The impactor is completely melted. The energy is above its latent heat of fusion, not merely enough to crater the surface.
  2. The molten material expands. This is the éktasis: the material loses its mechanical integrity and becomes part of a fluid, which is what allows it to mix rather than sit as an inclusion.
  3. The target survives. Not a disruption. The event increases the target’s mass and changes its composition.

Written as an energy window, with $Q_s$ the specific impact energy, $L_f$ the latent heat of fusion of the impactor and $Q_D^{*}$ the disruption threshold of the target:

$$ L_f ;\ll; Q_s ;\lesssim; Q_D^{*} $$

The lower bound is what separates meteoectasis from simple accretion. The upper bound is what separates it from fragmentation. In between is the regime where a collision homogenises two bodies.

Why the distinction earns its keep

Here is the case that motivates it. The Moon is widely believed to have formed from the debris of a giant impact with a Mars-sized body, conventionally called Theia. Under the standard model, a large part of the Moon derives from the impactor, and the impactor’s mass is diluted into the proto-Earth.

The problem is isotopic. Oxygen, titanium, tungsten and silicon isotope ratios in lunar and terrestrial samples are nearly identical. Two bodies that formed independently at different heliocentric distances should not be indistinguishable — different distances mean different proportions of the condensates available when each body accreted.

There is no shortage of proposed mechanisms: Theia formed at a similar distance; the system re-equilibrated through a vapour-rich disc; both bodies mixed in a common silicate reservoir; tidal processes finished the job. The mechanisms disagree with each other.

What they all have in common is that every one of them requires the impactor’s material to have been in a state where homogenisation is physically possible. Every one of them is a meteoectasis argument — they differ only on how the homogenisation took place, not on whether the event was capable of producing it.

That is what a name buys you. Without it, the debate reads as a debate about mechanism. With it, the shared premise becomes visible and the argument can be had where it actually is.

The defeat condition

A terminology proposal that cannot be abandoned is not a proposal, it is a preference. So the paper states the three ways this one dies:

  • The window is empty. If every impact energetic enough to melt the impactor also fragments the target, then meteoectasis never happens and the word names nothing. This is an empirical question about mass ratios and energy scaling, and it is answerable.
  • The word already exists. If the community already uses accretionary impact or perfect merger with exactly this meaning, a new term fragments the vocabulary instead of clarifying it, and the right move is to adopt the existing usage.
  • The distinction predicts nothing. If treating the impactor as a constituent and treating it as an inclusion give identical observable predictions for every quantity of interest, then the distinction is decoration. The paper claims they differ in isotopic budgets and in compositional stratification, and that claim can be checked.

None of these is a rhetorical hedge. They are the conditions under which I would withdraw the term, and I would rather write them down now than be asked for them later.

What this has to do with Brisecom

This is a planetary-science paper and Brisecom is not a planetary-science institute. The reason it exists here is the same reason the other twenty papers exist here: the failure mode being addressed is naming, not physics.

A field that describes two different physical states with one word will, sooner or later, model one as the other. I have watched this happen in software architectures, in AI governance, in cost accounting and in defence economics — always the same way: two distinct things get one name, and the difference disappears from the model before anyone notices it was load-bearing.

The paper’s contribution is a distinction, a window and a defeat condition. The physics was already there. What was missing was a word for the state.
